title: Be Prepared
description: A scouting motto becomes a comic catalogue of decidedly unscoutlike advice.
about: The narrator turns an earnest march into a portrait of youthful misbehavior. The contradictions are the joke: this is satirical character writing, not practical advice. This edition follows the four printed stanzas of the author's lyric sheet.
note: All four printed stanzas retained.

title: The Hunting Song
description: An unreliable hunter proudly recounts a disastrous day in the woods.
about: Repeated tallies and misplaced self-confidence drive this dark comic monologue. Its absurd narrator is not a model for real hunting behavior. The complete four-stanza text follows the author's published sheet.
note: All four printed stanzas retained.

title: I Hold Your Hand in Mine
description: The language of a sentimental love song conceals a macabre punchline.
about: Lehrer takes a familiar romantic expression literally, letting a gentle address turn into an unsettling fictional confession. The sixteen-line lyric is complete. A separate printed reference to another writer's parody is not part of the lyric and is excluded.
note: Only Lehrer's sixteen lyric lines are included; the footer advertising a separate Dr. H. Paul Shuch parody is excluded.

title: The Old Dope Peddler
description: A seemingly kindly neighborhood portrait turns into a satire of predatory commerce.
about: Cheerful phrasing clashes with the subject of the song, exposing the narrator's disturbing idea of doing good. This is a fictional satirical portrait, not an endorsement of drug sales. The four printed quatrains are reproduced in full.
note: All four printed quatrains retained.

title: Fight Fiercely, Harvard
description: A fight song whose determination keeps giving way to exaggerated politeness.
about: Tea invitations and timid asides undermine the usual rhetoric of sporting rivalry. Both printed stanzas, including their parenthetical interjections, are included. The wording follows the lyric sheet rather than any recording's spoken introduction.
note: Corrected two OCR artifacts against the rendered sheet; all parenthetical interjections retained.

This edition follows the complete first page, labeled recorded version; the separately labeled revised second page is not interleaved with it.

title: Alma
manualLines: The loveliest girl in Vienna
Was Alma --- the smartest as well.
Once you picked her up on your antenna,
You'd never be free of her spell.
Her lovers were many and varied
From the day she began her beguine.
There were three famous ones whom she married,
And God know how many between.
Alma, tell us, --- all modern women are jealous ---
Which of your magical wands
Got you Gustav and Walter and Franz?
The first one she married was Mahler,
Whose buddies all knew him as Gustav,
And each time he saw her he'd holler,
"Ach, dot is de fräulein I must have!"
Their marriage, however, was murder,
He'd scream to the heavens above,
"I'm writing 'Das Lied von der Erde,'
Und she only wants to make love!"
Alma, tell us, --- all modern women are jealous ---
You should have a statue in bronze
For bagging Gustav and Walter and Franz.
While married to Gus, she met Gropius,
And soon she was swinging with Walter.
Gus died, and her teardrops were copious.
She cried all the way to the altar.
But he would work late at the Bauhaus
And only came home now and then.
She said, "What am I running, a cow house?
It's time to change partners again."
Alma, tell us, --- all modern women are jealous ---
Though you didn't even use Ponds',
You got Gustav and Walter and Franz.
While married to Walt, she met Werfel,
And he too was caught in her net.
He married her, but he was carefel,
'Cause Alma was no Bernadette.
And that is the story of Alma,
Who knew how to receive and to give.
The body that reached her embalma
Was one that had known how to live.
Alma, tell us,
How can they help being jealous?
Ducks always envy the swans
Who get Gustav and Walter
You never did falter
With Gustav and Walter and Franz!
description: An elastic chain of names and rhymes turns a romantic life into a comic ballad.
about: The song frames Alma's marriages through Gustav, Walter, and Franz, using invented dialogue and deliberately distorted rhymes. It is a satirical portrait, not a complete biography. This edition was transcribed directly from the author's image-only sheet: all twelve indented blocks are present, including the extended final refrain and spellings such as carefel and embalma.
note: All 47 lines manually transcribed and visually checked against the single-page image-only PDF; source spellings and the umlaut are retained.

underlyingWork.rightsNote: The SGAE archive credits Felipe Pérez y González (1854–1910) as librettist and records the 1886 premiere; Spain's national library documents the nineteenth-century editions. The original lyric predates modern copyright terms, and Lehrer's English version is covered separately by his 2022 declaration. This does not license later recordings, photographs or editions.

description: A resourceful maid narrates her escape from exhausting work through an increasingly dubious education in survival.
about: This is Lehrer's English version of the maid's tango from La Gran Vía, with original Spanish words by Felipe Pérez y González and music by Federico Chueca and Joaquín Valverde. The left-hand English column supplies all six stanzas; the facing Spanish text is not interleaved. The narrator's schemes are theatrical satire. The final e-/Ven line break is preserved, and original-work evidence is separate from the translator's declaration.
note: Checked both columns and transcribed the complete fifty-one-line English version. Corrected three OCR spelling errors against the page, retained the split-word rhyme and excluded the separate performance-link note.

title: My Home Town
manualLines: I really have a yen
To go back once again,
Back to the place where no-one wears a frown,
To see once more those super-special just plain folks
In my home town.
No fellow could ignore
The little girl next door,
She sure looked sweet in her first evening gown.
Now there's a charge for what she used to give for free
In my home town.
I remember Dan, the druggist on the corner,
'E was never mean or ornery,
He was swell.
He killed his mother-in-law and ground her up real well,
And sprinkled just a bit
Over each banana split.
The guy that taught us math,
Who never took a bath,
Acquired a certain measure of renown,
And after school he sold the most amazing pictures
In my home town.
That fellow was no fool
Who taught our Sunday School,
And neither was our kindly Parson Brown.
(Hum)
In my home town.
I remember Sam, he was the village idiot
And though it seems a pity, it was so.
He loved to burn down houses just to watch the glow,
And nothing could be done
'Cause he was the mayor's son.
The guy that took a knife
And monogrammed his wife,
Then dropped her in the pond and watched her drown.
Oh, yes indeed, the people there are just plain folks
In my home town.

description: A nostalgic return to a small town reveals increasingly macabre stories behind its respectable neighbors.
about: The narrator's warm memories conceal grotesque stories about the people he grew up around. This is fictional dark satire, including violence and dated derogatory language. The author supplies a four-page score rather than a separate lyric sheet. This reading follows its upper lyric row, repeats with the lower row, then continues into the final coda. The written humming cue is retained without inventing words. Line breaks and the seven section titles are editorial reading aids; spoken introductions from recordings are not included.
